summary:
India's Parliament passed the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill in March 2026, replacing the 2019 law's self-identification route with legal recognition limited to historically accepted socio-cultural groups such as hijra and kinner, and to intersex individuals. Trans men, trans women and non-binary people who self-identify outside those categories fall outside the recognition scheme. Rights activists, among them Akkai Padmashali, describe the amendment as criminalising and an attack on the right to exist. The government presents it as widening access to welfare schemes and protection from trafficking; critics say it excludes many trans, non-binary and gender-fluid people. India has an estimated two million transgender people.

The baseline for entry and stay is mixed. Same-sex acts were decriminalised by the Supreme Court in 2018, and discrimination is barred on grounds including sex, interpreted to cover gender identity. Same-sex marriage and civil partnership are not available, although courts have acknowledged same-sex couples as family units.

Criminal-law protection weakened in 2024. Replacing the Indian Penal Code with the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita removed the gender-identity-specific offences that had shielded trans people from sexual violence, and trans communities report fear of a rise in assaults under the new code.

Checkpoint and document friction is documented across modes of travel. A trans woman at a Kolkata railway station alleged that a Railway Protection Force constable groped her under the pretext of checking her gender. Transgender people arrested by the Railway Protection Force in Assam recounted degrading treatment in custody in interviews recorded in June 2024. At Chennai International Airport Terminal 1 in November 2024, CISF personnel stopped an openly transgender law student, Sakshi Jain, although she presented a PAN card for verification. Passport authorities have required a trans applicant to sit a medical examination; the Allahabad High Court granted relief in February 2026.

The courts remain the strongest protection machinery. The Madras High Court's judgment of 7 June 2021 in S. Sushma v Commissioner of Police, delivered by Justice N. Anand Venkatesh, followed police harassment of a same-sex couple and issued sweeping guidelines covering police sensitisation, a ban on conversion therapy, and directions to the National Medical Commission and education authorities. The UK Home Office's country note of December 2025 records only limited reports of police abuse of LGBT+ people, likelier in conservative rural areas and not systemic.

For a visitor, exposure concentrates at checkpoints and in police contact rather than in statute alone: recognition narrowed in March 2026, sexual-violence safeguards removed in 2024, and abuse at railway, airport and passport encounters documented in 2024 and 2026, set against high courts that have intervened repeatedly on behalf of trans and LGBT+ people.
tangentialFactors:
The March 2026 amendment is contested on opposite readings of the same text. The government frames the shift away from self-identification as widening welfare access and strengthening anti-trafficking protection, while opponents inside and outside Parliament, including LGBTQ-community protesters, read it as exclusion of trans, non-binary and gender-fluid people from legal personhood.

Assessments of police conduct diverge in degree rather than in fact. The UK Home Office's December 2025 note characterises police abuse of LGBT+ people as limited and not systemic, and likelier in conservative rural areas, while the incident record from Kolkata, Assam and Chennai shows specific, named encounters with railway police, airport security and passport officials. Urban checkpoints are not exempt from the pattern the country note treats as peripheral.

Courts and the legislature are moving in opposite directions. The Supreme Court's 2018 decriminalisation, the Madras High Court's 2021 guidelines and the Allahabad High Court's 2026 relief on passport medical examinations sit against a Parliament that narrowed recognition in the same period, so the protective floor is judicial rather than statutory.

Scale matters for expectations: an estimated two million transgender people live in India, and the 2026 amendment determines which of them can evidence legal recognition at all.
localsOnly:
Residents' legal recognition is now governed by the 2019 Act as amended in March 2026, which ties recognition to historically accepted socio-cultural groups and to intersex status rather than to self-identification. Trans Indians who identified under the previous route face a change in how they evidence status for welfare schemes, employment and services.

The Madras High Court's 2021 guidelines in S. Sushma v Commissioner of Police bind police forces on sensitisation, prohibit conversion therapy, and direct the National Medical Commission and education authorities on treatment of LGBT+ people. These are domestic obligations with continuing effect on residents.

Discrimination on grounds including sex, read as covering gender identity, is prohibited in the fields the constitutional and statutory framework covers, and courts have recognised same-sex couples as family units for domestic purposes even though marriage and civil partnership remain unavailable.

Residents face the same custody and policing risks documented for travellers: the Assam Railway Protection Force detentions of June 2024 and the Kolkata station incident are domestic-facing examples of treatment in police hands.
outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved: the inventory does not state when the March 2026 amendment takes effect, whether rules or forms under it have been notified, or how it affects identity documents already issued to trans people.

Unresolved: whether the narrowed recognition scheme changes passport endorsements, visa applications or gender markers for foreign visitors is not addressed in any source here.

Unresolved: the inventory gives no figures on penalties for anti-trans violence under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, nor on prosecution rates for the offences the old Indian Penal Code did cover.

Unresolved: the frequency of airport, railway and passport incidents beyond the cited cases is not quantified, so the four documented encounters cannot be read as a rate.

Not sourced here: any count of state-level protection cells or other sub-national implementation machinery.
